1.why: Power is energy transferred divided by the time taken.

wrong.a: Energy used equals power times time.
wrong.d: Voltage times current is electrical power.

2.why: Watts measure power, which is energy per second.

3.why: Floating wind turbines can be deployed in deep ocean waters where shores are steep.

wrong.b: Wind speed decreases near the equator usually.
wrong.d: Wind farms stop working in light breezes.

story.title: Harnessing offshore winds
story.lead: Japan relies heavily on imported energy, with a self-sufficiency rate of just 16.4% [1]. Offshore wind power offers a sustainable domestic energy source [1].

story.body_1: Japan has immense potential for offshore wind energy along its extensive coastline [1]. Commercial projects have begun coming online, generating clean electricity for homes and businesses [1].
story.body_2: Because Japan has a narrow continental shelf, floating wind turbines are crucial for deep waters [1]. The Goto floating wind farm in Nagasaki prefecture recently began commercial operation [1].
timeline.1.text: Japan launches first floating wind project in Fukushima.
timeline.2.text: Commercial fixed-bottom offshore wind farms open in Akita.
timeline.3.text: Goto commercial floating wind farm begins operation in Nagasaki.
physics.title: Calculating power and energy
physics.body_1: Power tells us how fast energy is transferred or generated. When wind pushes turbine blades, they convert kinetic energy into electrical energy over time.
physics.body_2: Power is equal to the energy produced divided by the time taken. More energy in less time means greater power output.
physics.assumptions: We assume constant energy transfer rate and ignore mechanical friction losses.
table.note: Power equals energy generated divided by time.

lab.title: Pinwheel power test
lab.step_1: Make or hold a small paper pinwheel in front of a gentle fan or breeze.
lab.step_2: Count how many full rotations it makes in exactly 10 seconds.
lab.step_3: Calculate rotations per second to see how speed changes with wind.
lab.question: How did blowing harder change the rotations per second?
